title: Disaster Recovery Drill
intro: Twelve scenario questions on RTO and RPO, DR strategies, Route 53 routing and backup mechanics. Answer cold — the explanation appears after each choice.
footer: Drawn from Lab 08 — Failover and recovery points. Reference notes: exam-notes.md
notes_intro: Twelve SAA-C03-style questions on recovery objectives, DR strategies and DNS routing, then the traps and reference tables. Answers are at the bottom — try them cold first.

questions.q: A business states it can tolerate four hours of downtime but must not lose more than five minutes of data. Which pair of objectives does this describe?
options: RTO 5 minutes, RPO 4 hours
RTO 4 hours, RPO 5 minutes
Both RTO and RPO are 4 hours
RTO 4 hours, with no RPO requirement
questions.why: RTO is how long you are down — four hours here. RPO is how much data you may lose — five minutes. They are bought separately: a relaxed RTO permits a cheap strategy like pilot light, while a tight RPO demands continuous replication regardless.

questions.q: A company replicates its database continuously to a second region but keeps all application servers switched off there. In a disaster they start the servers and redirect traffic. Which DR strategy is this?
options: Backup and restore
Pilot light
Warm standby
Multi-site active/active
questions.why: Pilot light: the core data is always replicated and ready, but compute is off until needed. Recovery takes tens of minutes to start and scale. Warm standby keeps a scaled-down copy actually running. Backup and restore has nothing replicated continuously.

questions.q: A Route 53 failover record has a TTL of 3600 seconds. The health check detects failure in 60 seconds. What is the realistic worst-case recovery time for an already-connected client?
options: About 60 seconds
Up to roughly 61 minutes, because cached answers persist for the TTL
Immediate, because Route 53 pushes updates to resolvers
About 30 minutes, half the TTL
questions.why: Detection plus caching. Route 53 changes its answer after ~60 seconds, but resolvers that already answered keep serving the old value until their cached TTL expires — up to an hour. The TTL is a floor on recovery time you set in advance, which is why failover records use short TTLs.

questions.q: Which Route 53 routing policy sends users to the region that gives them the lowest response time?
options: Geolocation
Latency-based
Geoproximity
Weighted
questions.why: Latency-based routing uses measured latency between the user and AWS regions. Geolocation routes by where the user is, which is about compliance and localisation rather than speed. Geoproximity routes by distance with an adjustable bias. Weighted splits by proportion, for canaries and migrations.

questions.q: An engineer accidentally deletes rows from a DynamoDB table at 14:30. Point-in-time recovery is enabled. What can they do?
options: Undo the deletion in place on the existing table
Restore to a new table as it existed at any second within the last 35 days
Restore only from the most recent daily snapshot
Nothing — PITR only protects against infrastructure failure
questions.why: PITR restores to a new table — never in place — at any second within the trailing 35 days. Note that it protects against application errors as much as infrastructure failure; a bad deploy writing garbage is the common case. The restore target being a new table means cutover is a deliberate step.

questions.q: Which statement about enabling S3 versioning and DynamoDB PITR is correct?
options: Both can be enabled after an incident to recover prior data
Both must be enabled before the incident — they cannot recover data lost beforehand
Versioning is retroactive but PITR is not
Both are enabled by default on new resources
questions.why: Neither is retroactive. Versioning starts preserving versions from the moment it is switched on; PITR starts its continuous backup window then too. Turning them on after the mistake recovers nothing — which is why recovery point is a decision made long before the disaster, and why neither being on by default is worth knowing.

questions.q: A Route 53 health check monitors an endpoint that returns 200 from a load balancer even when the database behind it is failing. What is the consequence?
options: Route 53 fails over as soon as user requests error
The health check keeps passing, failover never triggers, and the outage continues
The health check times out and triggers failover
CloudWatch automatically overrides the health check
questions.why: A health check only knows what the checked path tells it. A shallow check on / that does not touch the failing dependency keeps passing while the application is broken, so failover never happens. The check must exercise the dependency you are actually worried about — the same lesson as ALB health checks in Lab 02.

questions.q: Which DR strategy has the lowest RTO, and what is the trade-off?
options: Backup and restore — lowest cost and lowest RTO
Multi-site active/active — near-zero RTO, at roughly double the running cost
Pilot light — near-zero RTO, at minimal cost
Warm standby — zero RTO with no additional cost
questions.why: Multi-site active/active serves live traffic from both regions, so recovery is effectively immediate — and you pay for full capacity in both, plus the hardest engineering problem: keeping data consistent when both sides accept writes. RTO and cost trade against each other across all four strategies.

questions.q: An application needs a relational database with cross-region disaster recovery, an RPO of about one second, and promotion of the secondary region in under a minute. What fits?
options: RDS Multi-AZ
Aurora Global Database
RDS cross-region read replica
DynamoDB global tables
questions.why: Aurora Global Database replicates cross-region with typically sub-second lag and promotes a secondary region in about a minute. RDS Multi-AZ is single-region and solves AZ failure only. A cross-region read replica works but has higher lag and slower manual promotion. DynamoDB global tables are excellent but not relational.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an S3 delete marker in a versioned bucket?
options: It permanently erases all versions of the object
It becomes the current version so the object appears deleted, while prior versions remain
It marks the object for lifecycle transition to Glacier
It prevents the object from being deleted
questions.why: A delete on a versioned bucket inserts a delete marker as the new current version. The object appears gone, but every prior version still exists and still bills. Removing the marker restores the object — and this is also why a versioned bucket is not truly empty when teardown tries to delete it.

questions.q: A company wants to centrally define and enforce backup schedules and retention across EC2, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB and EFS. Which service is designed for this?
options: Amazon S3 lifecycle policies
AWS Backup
AWS Config
Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager
questions.why: AWS Backup centralises backup plans, schedules, retention and cross-region copy across many services, with vaults and compliance reporting. Data Lifecycle Manager handles EBS snapshots only. Config reports on configuration compliance but takes no backups.

questions.q: Which Route 53 routing policy would you use to send 10% of traffic to a new version of an application?
options: Failover
Weighted
Multivalue answer
Geolocation
questions.why: Weighted routing splits traffic by assigned proportions — the standard mechanism for canary releases and gradual migrations. Failover is active/passive. Multivalue returns up to eight healthy answers and is a poor substitute for a load balancer. Geolocation routes by user location.
